---
title: "Focal Trees"
subtitle: "100 candidate holly trees balanced across urbanization and landscape heterogeneity"
date: today
---

```{r setup}
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(leaflet)
library(plotly)
library(terra)
library(here)

source(here("R", "functions.R"))
derived <- here(cfg$paths$derived)
fc <- cfg$focal

line    <- load_transect()
aoi     <- load_aoi()
focal   <- st_read(file.path(derived, "focal_trees.gpkg"), quiet = TRUE)
bins    <- read.csv(file.path(derived, "focal_bins.csv"))
loads   <- read.csv(file.path(derived, "landscape_pca.csv"))
land    <- rast(file.path(derived, "landscape_30m.tif"))
prim    <- focal[focal$role == "primary", ]

bin_pal <- colorRampPalette(c("#1b7837", "#a6dba0", "#f7f7f7", "#c2a5cf", "#762a83"))(fc$n_bins)
bin_lab <- sprintf("%d: %.0f–%.0f%%", bins$bin, bins$imperv_from, bins$imperv_to)
```

## Purpose

Field work needs a fixed set of focal trees: holly that will be mapped, sexed, and followed for
seed set, herbivory, and pollinators. This page picks `r fc$n_trees` of them from the holly
candidates, plus ranked alternates, so that:

- they are **spread evenly across the urbanization gradient**, from forest to downtown;
- within each part of the gradient they **span landscape heterogeneity** (mixed versus uniform
  surroundings) and **distance along the transect**;
- no two listed trees are closer than **`r fc$min_spacing_m` m**, to reduce the chance of
  sampling parent–offspring pairs or sibships from the same seed shadow.

| Step | Script | Output |
|---|---|---|
| 10. Landscape metrics, indices, selection | `R/08_focal_trees.R` | `data/derived/landscape_30m.tif`, `focal_bins.csv`, `focal_trees.{gpkg,csv,gpx}` |

::: {.callout-important}
## Candidates, not confirmed holly

These are crowns that the imagery flags as small, isolated evergreens. Some will be other
species, especially on developed land (magnolia, cedar, boxwood, other ornamentals). Each bin
therefore has `r fc$alternates_per_bin` ranked alternates. If a primary is not holly, or cannot be
accessed, use the next alternate in the **same bin**. All `r nrow(focal)` listed trees respect the
spacing rule, so any substitution keeps it.
:::

## Pool

The pool is every crown that passes the size (`r cfg$holly$candidate_diam_ft[1]`–`r cfg$holly$candidate_diam_ft[2]` ft)
and isolation (evergreen share ≤ `r cfg$holly$context_max`) parts of the candidate rule, not cut
by a tile edge. Unlike the [holly candidate list](03_holly_classification.qmd), **developed land
is included**: without it the urban end of the transect (km 0–4) has almost no candidates. Only
open water is excluded. Pool size: `r format(sum(bins$pool_crowns), big.mark = ",")` crowns.

## Landscape context

Each crown is described by its surroundings within **`r fc$buffer_m` m**, computed on the native
30 m Annual NLCD grid (`r cfg$nlcd$year`):

| Metric | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `imperv_mean` | mean fractional impervious surface (%) |
| `imperv_sd` | standard deviation of impervious surface among cells: patchiness of development |
| `forest_pct`, `developed_pct` | share of forest (41–43) and developed (21–24) cover |
| `shdi` | Shannon diversity of grouped land cover (developed, developed open, forest, wetland, water, ...) |
| `shei` | Shannon evenness: diversity relative to its maximum for the classes present (0 = one class, 1 = all equal) |
| `edge_density` | metres of boundary between grouped cover types per hectare |

Two indices are used:

- **Urbanization index** = `imperv_mean`. A PCA of all metrics was tried first, but its first
  axis saturated at the urban end: forest and developed shares reach 0% and 100% well before
  the urban core, so it could not separate suburbs from downtown. Impervious surface keeps
  rising all the way to the core.
- **Heterogeneity index** = first principal component of
  `r paste(loads$metric, collapse = ", ")` across all 30 m cells in the study area
  (`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * loads$var_explained[1])` of their variance). Higher values mean
  more mixed, more evenly divided, more fragmented surroundings.

```{r loadings}
loads |>
  transmute(Metric = metric, Loading = round(loading, 2)) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

```{r index-maps, fig.width=10, fig.height=6}
aoi_lc <- vect(st_transform(aoi, crs(land)))
idx <- mask(crop(land[[c("urban_index", "heterogeneity_index")]], aoi_lc), aoi_lc)
pts <- vect(st_transform(prim, crs(land)))
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(idx[["urban_index"]], main = "Urbanization index (impervious %, 500 m)", axes = FALSE,
     col = hcl.colors(50, "Purple-Orange", rev = TRUE), mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 2, 4))
plot(pts, add = TRUE, pch = 21, col = "black", bg = "white", cex = 1.1)
plot(idx[["heterogeneity_index"]], main = "Heterogeneity index", axes = FALSE,
     col = hcl.colors(50, "YlGnBu", rev = TRUE), mar = c(0.5, 0.5, 2, 4))
plot(pts, add = TRUE, pch = 21, col = "black", bg = "white", cex = 1.1)
```

Heterogeneity is **hump-shaped** along the gradient: it is low in continuous forest and in the
downtown core, and highest at intermediate urbanization (about 10–25% impervious), where
houses, lawns, roads, and forest patches are interleaved. The two indices therefore describe
different things, and a design that balanced on land-cover fractions alone would sample the
peri-urban mix without controlling for it.

## Selection

The urbanization index is cut into `r fc$n_bins` bins and each bin gets
`r fc$n_trees / fc$n_bins` primaries and `r fc$alternates_per_bin` alternates. The bins are of
equal width on the **arcsine-square-root** scale of the impervious fraction, the standard
transform for proportions. Equal-width bins on raw impervious % put the whole forest end
(0–10%) into one bin and most of the sample into the city; the transform gives the forest end
and the urban core similar resolution.

```{r bins}
bins |>
  left_join(count(st_drop_geometry(prim), bin, name = "primaries"), by = "bin") |>
  transmute(Bin = bin, `Impervious (%)` = sprintf("%.1f–%.1f", imperv_from, imperv_to),
            `Pool crowns` = format(pool_crowns, big.mark = ","), Primaries = primaries) |>
  knitr::kable(align = "lrrr")
```

Within each bin, trees are added one at a time. Each new tree is the eligible crown farthest
(in standardized heterogeneity index and distance along the transect) from the trees already
chosen in that bin, so a bin's trees span both. A crown is eligible only if it is at least
`r fc$min_spacing_m` m from every tree already listed in any bin. Bins with the fewest crowns are
filled first so that the spacing rule does not crowd them out. The first tree in each bin is
random (seed `r fc$seed` in `config.yml`), so a rerun gives the same list.

### Coverage

```{r coverage, fig.width=9, fig.height=5}
pool_s <- as.data.frame(mask(land[[c("urban_index", "heterogeneity_index")]], aoi_lc), na.rm = TRUE)
pool_s <- pool_s[sample(nrow(pool_s), min(20000, nrow(pool_s))), ]
ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = pool_s, aes(urban_index, heterogeneity_index), colour = "grey80", size = 0.3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = bins$imperv_from[-1], colour = "grey60", linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_point(data = st_drop_geometry(focal), aes(urban_index, heterogeneity_index, shape = role,
                                                  fill = factor(bin)), size = 2.2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = bin_pal, labels = bin_lab, name = "Bin (impervious)") +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(primary = 21, alternate = 24), name = NULL) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(override.aes = list(shape = 21))) +
  labs(x = "Urbanization index (impervious %, 500 m)", y = "Heterogeneity index",
       caption = "Grey: 30 m cells in the study area. Dotted lines: bin edges.") +
  theme_minimal() + theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

```{r along, fig.width=9, fig.height=3}
ggplot(st_drop_geometry(prim), aes(u_km, urban_index, fill = factor(bin))) +
  geom_point(shape = 21, size = 2.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = bin_pal, labels = bin_lab, name = "Bin") +
  labs(x = "Distance from Richmond (km)", y = "Impervious %") +
  theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "none", panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

Primaries are spread along the whole transect, but not evenly by kilometre. The most urban bins
(8–10) lie within the first ~14 km and the least urban bin entirely beyond km 22, while the
intermediate bins are spread along most of the route, because suburban and peri-urban land recurs
all along it (including the corridor of higher development near km 9–11). That is the intended
trade-off of balancing on the gradient rather than on distance.

### Spacing

```{r spacing}
# Centre-to-centre distances, as used by the spacing rule
d <- st_distance(st_centroid(st_geometry(focal)))
units(d) <- "m"
d <- matrix(as.numeric(d), nrow(focal))
diag(d) <- Inf
nn <- apply(d, 1, min)
nn_p <- apply(d[focal$role == "primary", focal$role == "primary"], 1, min)
```

The closest pair of listed trees is `r sprintf("%.0f", min(nn))` m apart (crown centre to
centre). Among primaries only,
the median distance to the nearest other primary is `r sprintf("%.0f", median(nn_p))` m
(range `r sprintf("%.0f", min(nn_p))`–`r sprintf("%.0f", max(nn_p))` m).

## Map

Primaries are circles and alternates are triangles (smaller), coloured by bin. Click a tree for
its id and context.

```{r map}
ll <- st_transform(st_centroid(focal), 4326)
ll$col <- bin_pal[ll$bin]
ll$popup <- sprintf(
  "<b>%s</b> (%s, bin %d)<br>Crown %s, %.0f ft<br>Impervious %.1f%% | forest %.0f%%<br>
   Heterogeneity %.2f | evenness %.2f | edge %.0f m/ha<br>%.1f km along transect<br>%.6f, %.6f",
  ll$focal_id, ll$role, ll$bin, ll$obj_id, ll$diam_ft, ll$imperv_mean, ll$forest_pct,
  ll$heterogeneity_index, ll$shei, ll$edge_density, ll$u_km, ll$lat, ll$lon)
pal <- colorFactor(bin_pal, levels = seq_len(fc$n_bins))
leaflet() |>
  addProviderTiles(providers$Esri.WorldImagery, group = "Imagery",
                   options = providerTileOptions(maxNativeZoom = 19, maxZoom = 21)) |>
  addProviderTiles(providers$Esri.WorldGrayCanvas, group = "Light") |>
  addPolygons(data = st_transform(aoi, 4326), color = "white", weight = 1, fill = FALSE) |>
  addPolylines(data = st_transform(line, 4326), color = "white", dashArray = "6", weight = 2) |>
  addCircleMarkers(data = ll[ll$role == "alternate", ], radius = 3, color = ~col, weight = 1,
                   fillOpacity = 0.6, popup = ~popup, group = "Alternates") |>
  addCircleMarkers(data = ll[ll$role == "primary", ], radius = 6, color = "black", weight = 1,
                   fillColor = ~col, fillOpacity = 0.9, popup = ~popup, group = "Primaries") |>
  addLegend(colors = bin_pal, labels = bin_lab, title = "Bin (impervious)", opacity = 0.9) |>
  addLayersControl(baseGroups = c("Imagery", "Light"), overlayGroups = c("Primaries", "Alternates")) |>
  hideGroup("Alternates")
```

## Primary trees

```{r table}
prim |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  arrange(bin, u_km) |>
  transmute(ID = focal_id, Bin = bin, `km` = round(u_km, 1), `Impervious %` = round(imperv_mean, 1),
            `Forest %` = round(forest_pct), Heterogeneity = round(heterogeneity_index, 2),
            `Crown (ft)` = round(diam_ft), Lat = round(lat, 6), Lon = round(lon, 6)) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

The full list with alternates is `data/derived/focal_trees.csv` (and `.gpx` for GPS units and
phone apps). Each row carries the crown id from the candidate run, so field records can be
joined back to imagery features.

## Notes

- **Spacing.** `r fc$min_spacing_m` m is a working choice. Holly fruit is bird-dispersed, and
  most seeds of bird-dispersed trees fall within a few hundred metres of the parent, so trees
  100 m apart can still be related. A genetic check (e.g. a kinship estimate from markers) on
  the final set would show how much residual relatedness remains. Increase `min_spacing_m` in
  `config.yml` and rerun `R/08_focal_trees.R` (about 30 s) to tighten it.
- **Scale.** Landscape context uses a `r fc$buffer_m` m radius, a common scale for urban
  landscape effects on plants and their insects. Pollinator and leaf-miner responses may work at
  other scales; the metrics can be recomputed at several radii for analysis without changing the
  tree list.
- **Access.** Urban bins fall largely on private land (yards, institutional grounds). Expect
  more substitutions there, from both access and ornamental look-alikes.
- **NLCD limits.** Context comes from 30 m NLCD, so small features (a single street tree's
  yard, a narrow riparian strip) are blurred. Neighbourhoods near the edge of the NLCD extract
  are truncated.
